Preparing your data

Source: vignettes/preparing_data.Rmd
preparing_data.Rmd
library(bisonR)

This article describes the data format used by bisonR and how to convert common types of data to it.

The basic format

bison_model() takes a data frame in which each row contains observations of one pair of individuals (a dyad). This is similar to an edge list, but contains the observation data from which edge weights are estimated rather than the edge weights themselves:

Column Meaning
Node 1, node 2 The two individuals in the dyad. Names or IDs.
Event How many social events were seen: 0/1 for binary data, or a count.
Effort How much the dyad was observed: number of sampling periods, hours of observation, etc.
Anything else Optional predictors, such as location, observer or individual traits. 
df <- data.frame(
  node_1 = c("Ada", "Ada", "Ada", "Bea", "Bea", "Cat"),
  node_2 = c("Bea", "Cat", "Dot", "Cat", "Dot", "Dot"),
  together = c(8, 1, 0, 5, 2, 9),
  periods = c(10, 10, 4, 10, 4, 12)
)
df
#>   node_1 node_2 together periods
#> 1    Ada    Bea        8      10
#> 2    Ada    Cat        1      10
#> 3    Ada    Dot        0       4
#> 4    Bea    Cat        5      10
#> 5    Bea    Dot        2       4
#> 6    Cat    Dot        9      12

Here together is the number of sampling periods in which each pair were seen together, and periods is the number of sampling periods in which they could have been seen together. These columns are given on the left-hand side of the formula:

fit <- bison_model(
  (together | periods) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2),
  data = df,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)
summary(fit)
#> === Fitted BISoN edge model ===
#> Data type: binary
#> Formula: (together | periods) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2)
#> Number of nodes: 4
#> Number of dyads: 6
#> Directed: FALSE
#> === Edge list summary ===
#>             median    5%   95%
#> Ada <-> Bea  0.765 0.528 0.922
#> Ada <-> Cat  0.146 0.032 0.369
#> Ada <-> Dot  0.132 0.011 0.454
#> Bea <-> Cat  0.501 0.275 0.725
#> Bea <-> Dot  0.503 0.187 0.808
#> Cat <-> Dot  0.719 0.506 0.886

Ada and Dot were observed in only 4 periods, so their edge weight is less certain than that of Ada and Cat (10 periods), although both pairs have low point estimates.

What “effort” means

Effort is how much each dyad was observed, for example the number of scans that included both individuals, or the number of hours they were both under observation. It tells the model how much information there is about each edge weight: the more a dyad was observed, the more certain its edge weight.

If every row has the same effort, it can be written as a number instead of a column: (event | 1) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2).

Node names

Node names can be characters, numbers or factors. If both node columns are factors with the same levels, every level is treated as a node, including any that do not appear in the data. Otherwise, the nodes are the names that appear in the data, plus the levels of a node column that is a factor.

Binary or count data?

  • Use a binary model (model_type = "binary") when each sampling period records whether a social event happened or not, such as being seen in the same group during a scan. The edge weight is the probability of an event in a sampling period. Events can’t exceed effort.
  • Use a count model (model_type = "count") when you count interactions, such as the number of grooming bouts during focal follows. The edge weight is the rate of events per unit effort (for example, per hour). Effort doesn’t need to be a whole number.
df_counts <- data.frame(
  node_1 = c("Ada", "Ada", "Bea"),
  node_2 = c("Bea", "Cat", "Cat"),
  grooming_bouts = c(12, 0, 3),
  hours_observed = c(5.5, 2, 6.25)
)
fit_counts <- bison_model(
  (grooming_bouts | hours_observed) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2),
  data = df_counts,
  model_type = "count_conjugate",
  priors = get_default_priors("count_conjugate")
)
get_edgelist(fit_counts)
#>   node_1 node_2 median    5%   95%
#> 1    Ada    Bea  1.923 1.169 2.966
#> 2    Ada    Cat  0.235 0.017 1.033
#> 3    Bea    Cat  0.498 0.180 1.065

bisonR doesn’t yet have a model for the length of interactions (for example, minutes spent grooming). For now, convert_duration_to_binary() can turn this kind of data into binary data by splitting time into fixed-length periods. This is an approximation and should be used with caution.

Aggregated or disaggregated?

Data can have one row per observation (disaggregated) or one row per dyad, with events and effort summed (aggregated). Both give the same edge weights, but differ in what else can be included in the model:

  • Observation-level predictors, such as the location or time of day of each sampling period, need disaggregated data, since they vary between rows of the same dyad.
  • Aggregated data are much faster to fit with Stan. (Conjugate models give the same results for aggregated and disaggregated data.)

Data can be aggregated as far as possible while keeping the predictors that are needed. For example, if location is the only observation-level predictor, the data can be aggregated to one row per dyad per location:

sim <- simulate_bison_model("binary", aggregated = FALSE)
df_obs <- sim$df_sim
nrow(df_obs)
#> [1] 135

df_by_location <- aggregate(cbind(event, effort) ~ node_1_id + node_2_id + location, data = df_obs, FUN = sum)
nrow(df_by_location)
#> [1] 96
head(df_by_location)
#>   node_1_id node_2_id location event effort
#> 1         2         3        1     0      2
#> 2         2         4        1     2      3
#> 3         3         4        1     0      2
#> 4         3         5        1     1      2
#> 5         2         6        1     0      1
#> 6         3         6        1     0      1

Undirected and directed networks

By default, networks are undirected: the edge between A and B is the same as the edge between B and A, and rows can list the pair in either order.

df_undirected <- data.frame(
  node_1 = c("Ada", "Bea"), node_2 = c("Bea", "Ada"), event = c(3, 2), effort = c(5, 5)
)
fit_undirected <- bison_model(
  (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2), data = df_undirected,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate", priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)
#> 1 dyad(s) have rows in both orders (e.g. A, B and B, A). Because directed = FALSE, both orders are combined into one edge. If node_1 and node_2 are an actor and a receiver, use directed = TRUE.
get_edgelist(fit_undirected) # One edge, using all 5 events in 10 periods
#>   node_1 node_2 median   5%   95%
#> 1    Ada    Bea  0.501 0.27 0.733

For behaviours with an actor and a receiver, such as grooming or aggression, use directed = TRUE. Then node_1 is the actor and node_2 the receiver, and A → B and B → A are separate edges with their own weights:

fit_directed <- bison_model(
  (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2), data = df_undirected, directed = TRUE,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate", priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)
get_edgelist(fit_directed)
#>   node_1 node_2 median    5%   95%
#> 1    Ada    Bea  0.582 0.272 0.847
#> 2    Bea    Ada  0.420 0.152 0.733

The effort for each direction should be how much that behaviour could have been observed in that direction, for example in hours or sampling periods. Edges are only estimated for the directions that appear in the data, so rows with 0 events should be included for directions in which the behaviour was never seen.

Dyads that were never observed

Dyads with no rows in the data are not included in the model. If both individuals were present but never seen together, include a row with 0 events and the corresponding effort. Dyads that could never have been observed together should be left out.

Group-by-individual data

Gambit-of-the-group data (where individuals seen in the same group are assumed to be associating) are often stored as a group-by-individual (GBI) matrix, where each row is a group or sampling event and each column an individual, with 1 if the individual was present:

gbi <- matrix(rbinom(30 * 6, 1, 0.4), nrow = 30, ncol = 6,
              dimnames = list(NULL, c("Ada", "Bea", "Cat", "Dot", "Eve", "Fay")))
head(gbi)
#>      Ada Bea Cat Dot Eve Fay
#> [1,]   1   0   0   0   1   1
#> [2,]   1   1   0   1   0   1
#> [3,]   0   0   1   1   0   1
#> [4,]   1   1   0   0   1   1
#> [5,]   0   0   0   0   1   1
#> [6,]   1   0   0   0   0   1

convert_gbi_to_bison() converts this to the bisonR format. For each pair of individuals and each group in which at least one of the pair was present, it adds a row with event = 1 if both were present and event = 0 if only one was. Groups in which neither was present are not included. Each row is one sampling period, so the effort is 1:

df_gbi <- convert_gbi_to_bison(gbi)
head(df_gbi)
#>   node_1 node_2 event group_id
#> 1    Ada    Bea     0        1
#> 2    Ada    Bea     1        2
#> 3    Ada    Bea     1        4
#> 4    Ada    Bea     0        6
#> 5    Ada    Bea     0        7
#> 6    Ada    Bea     0        8

fit_gbi <- bison_model(
  (event | 1) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2),
  data = df_gbi,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)

Group-level information (such as location) can be added with group_properties, and individual traits with individual_properties. If some pairs could not have been seen together, for example because they were in the study area at different times, use individual_constraints to give each individual a value. Only pairs with the same value are then included.

Rows from the same group are not independent, so a random effect of group can be added to a (non-conjugate) model with + (1 | group_id).

Common errors

bison_model() checks the data before fitting. The most common errors are:

  • Columns not found: the names in the formula must exactly match columns in the data.
  • Missing values: remove rows with NA in any column used by the model, or impute (fill in) the missing values.
  • More events than sampling periods: in binary models, the number of events cannot exceed the effort. Use a count model for counts of interactions.
  • Self-loops: rows where both nodes are the same individual aren’t allowed.
